title: Why one ether synthesis works and the other fails
asks: Two ways of joining the same two pieces are tried. One gives the ether, the other does not. Explain with structures and mechanisms.

know.h: The Williamson ether synthesis is an {{SN2}} reaction. An alkoxide ({{RO-}}) attacks the carbon that carries a leaving group from the back, and the leaving group leaves in the same step: two arrows, no intermediate.
know.from: Lecture 11/05, p. 1 (reaction C); FA24 Exam 2, Q5A

know.h: Every unsymmetrical ether can be cut two ways. For R-O-R', the oxygen can arrive on R ({{RO-}} with R'-X) or on R' ({{R'O-}} with R-X). The pieces are the same; only the piece that carries the leaving group changes.
The carbon that carries the leaving group decides. {{SN2}} rates: methyl 1, ethyl (primary) 0.033, isopropyl (secondary) 0.00083, tert-butyl (tertiary) 0. Tertiary halides never do {{SN2}}.
Alkoxides are strong bases. Their conjugate acids are alcohols: methanol {{pKa}} 15.5, ethanol 15.9, isopropanol 16.5, tert-butanol 17.0. Where {{SN2}} is slow, a strong base eliminates instead.
Strong base with a tertiary halide gives {{E2}} only. In lecture, tert-butyl bromide with NaOH gave 2-methylpropene and no alcohol: rate = k[RBr][base].
Strong base with a secondary halide gives mostly {{E2}}. 2-Bromopropane with ethoxide gives mostly propene and only a little ether.

The {{E2}} mechanism has three arrows: base lone pair to a beta hydrogen, the C-H bond to the new C=C, the C-X bond to X. The hydrogen and the leaving group are anti-periplanar. The products are the alkene, the conjugate acid of the base (an alcohol) and the halide ion.

A methyl halide can only substitute. It has no beta hydrogen, so {{E2}} is impossible, and a methyl cation never forms, so there is no {{SN1}} or {{E1}}. A benzyl halide also has no beta hydrogen on an {{sp3}} carbon.
Bulk hurts far more on the halide than on the alkoxide. tert-Butoxide is a poor nucleophile, yet it still attacks the open carbon of {{CH3I}} and gives tert-butyl methyl ether.
know.from: Lecture 11/05, p. 1 and 3; FA24 Exam 2, Q5A

know.h: A bulky strong base with a primary halide that has beta hydrogens is sent to {{E2}} by the flowchart. So the safest partner for a bulky alkoxide is a methyl halide.

No {{SN2}} and no {{SN1}} at an {{sp2}} carbon (vinyl or aryl: rate 0). An aryl ether must be made from the phenoxide ({{ArO-}}) and an alkyl halide. Phenol has {{pKa}} 10, so its anion is easy to make and is a weak base.
know.from: Lecture 11/10, Figure 7.3; FA24 Exam 2, Q2A and Q1A

know.h: Two alcohols do not make an ether this way. A neutral alcohol is a poor nucleophile ({{CH3OH}} 1 against {{HO-}} 16,000) and {{HO-}} is a strong base and a poor leaving group.

Skills: draw the {{SN2}} step with two arrows, draw the {{E2}} step with three arrows, and write the products the failed route really gives. A stereocentre on the alkoxide carbon is untouched, because no bond to it is made or broken.

method: Cut the ether on each side of the oxygen and write the two alkoxide and halide pairs.
In each pair, classify the carbon that carries the leaving group: methyl, primary, secondary, tertiary or {{sp2}}.
Pick the pair whose halide is methyl or primary, best of all one with no beta hydrogen. The branched or ring piece goes in the alkoxide.
For the pair that works, draw the {{SN2}} step: oxygen lone pair to carbon from the back, C-X bond to X, and the ether as product.
For the pair that fails, say why {{SN2}} cannot happen (three alkyl groups block the back of a tertiary carbon, or the carbon is {{sp2}}).

Then say what happens instead: an alkoxide is a strong base, so draw the {{E2}} step with three arrows and write the alkene, the alcohol and the halide ion. If the carbon is {{sp2}}, write no reaction.
Finish with the lesson in one line: methyl or primary halide, bulky group in the alkoxide.

pitfalls.h: Judging the route by the bulk of the alkoxide. The class of the halide carbon decides: tert-butoxide with {{CH3I}} works, methoxide with a tertiary halide does not.
Writing "no reaction" for an alkoxide with a tertiary halide. {{E2}} does happen: draw the alkene, the alcohol and the halide ion.
Calling the failed route {{SN1}} or {{E1}}. A strong base is present, so it removes a beta hydrogen in one step before the halide can ionize.
Drawing the {{E2}} arrow from the base to carbon, or leaving out the conjugate acid of the base (methanol from methoxide) in the products.
Explaining only the reaction that works. Most of the points are for why the other fails and what it gives.
Inverting a stereocentre that belongs to the alkoxide. Inversion happens at the carbon that is attacked, which is on the halide.
